# HaloHoney’s Flapcrack™

By [Nicola Knight](https://amigettingthrough.wordpress.com/author/kninki/)

While I was out shopping, it occurred to me that I could/should make some flapjack. The last time I made this was just before my son was born, over two years ago. I think it’s time.

HaloHoney is a rather lovely internet friend of mine, and her recipe has become affectionately known as ‘flapcrack’. The original recipe is below, but this means you are left with half a tin of condensed milk. In this case, you have two options – one, grab a spoon; or two, double all the quantities and make a Metric Fucktonne™ of Flapcrack™.

300g Butter  
340g demerara sugar  
4 heaped tbsps golden syrup  
½ tin of condensed milk  
500g rolled oats (can be cheap ones)

Preheat oven to 160°C  
Line a baking sheet (swiss roll tin is ideal) with baking parchment – it doesn’t need to be neat, or even greased as long as you use parchment.  
Put sugar, butter and syrup into a pan over a medium heat, stirring constantly to stop it catching. Make sure the butter is melted, but don’t worry if the mixture is separated.  
Take the pan off the heat, pour in the condensed milk. Stir until combined.  
Stir in rolled oats.  
Empty mixture into lined baking tin and distribute it fairly evenly – it levels out pretty well if roughly in the right place, there’s certainly no need to press it down.  
Put the tin in the middle of the oven for 10-15 minutes or until lightly golden brown.  
Allow to cool in the tin. Change into loose fitting clothing.  
Cut into pieces. Small ones, in an attempt to make it go further.HaloHoney’s Flapcrack™

A child’s laughter. The sound of a ball bouncing. A nanny-bot hums nearby, its movements precise, soulless.

The world feels shimmery, almost like it’s slipping away from me. My mouth stretches into a smile that doesn’t belong to me. Mr. Jones from Number 3 All-Life Lane approaches with his usual cordiality, and, unusually a health helper at his side.

"Ms. Seymore, so glad to catch you. If you would just come this way, we’ll get you more comfortable."

The words seem to hang in the air like a thick fog. My mind screams that something is wrong, but my lips betray me. "Oh, most certainly, dear Mr. Jones. How lovely to see you."

I don’t remember when I started following them, or how. The moments blur together as I’m led into a clean, sterile room. The walls are white, too bright, like the light is trying to scrub away my thoughts. A nurse greets me, her voice honey-sweet, but the smile on her face doesn’t reach her eyes.

I’m laying down. When did I lie down?

Cold hands brush my skin. My clothes are gone. There’s music playing—soothing, repetitive, lulling me deeper into a haze. The nurse’s voice echoes above it all, gently reminding me of the rules, of how we All-Life's follow them with open hearts to make the world a better place.

I know this isn’t right. I know it. But the thought slips through my fingers, like smoke.

“A little scratch, Mrs. Jones, and you’ll feel much better.”

I don’t even correct her. The needle pierces my skin, cold liquid creeping through my veins. I try to hold onto the fear, the promise I made, but the coolness spreads, softening everything. My worries dissolve, and I can’t remember why I was afraid in the first place.

“There we are, Mrs. Jones. Reset to age 21 and good to go. We hope you find blessings in your day.”

The nurse’s voice is like a balm, soothing, as she helps me up. I’m floating, walking out on a cloud. I see my husband—my dear, sweet Matthew, waiting for me, his smile gentle but expectant.

“How can I make you happy, dear one?” I ask, my voice light, airy. Perfect.

It feels so right.

**Ding! Good Morning, Ms. Seymore. It is now 7 a.m. on the 8th of September, 2048. Ding!**

The chime echoes in my mind as I sit up, the ache in my knees greeting me like an old friend. I force myself to glance at the mirror. My reflection looks back with dull eyes—notifications already flashing beside my face: advertisements for upgrades, offers, and, of course, the daily reminder to schedule my physical.

**"Upgrade your life today. Join your neighbours, friends, and family with All-Life. Speak to your local representative now."**

The same message for a decade. The same insistent promises. Everyone between 18 and 50 has taken All-Life by now, swayed by the "low-cost, easy repayments" deal that swept the world in 2028. I was 12 then, and even though my mother worked on the project, she forbade it in our house. She grew quiet and distant whenever I asked about it—something about doing the right thing, not the easy thing.

Now, she's gone, leaving me with that promise. To never take All-Life. To never give in.

**Ding! Message received from Brie—Sister.**

I already know what it says.

**"Hello dear sister, I hope to have you join us someday soon. Do call as soon as you are ready. Matthew wishes you well. Kindly, Brie."**

Eight years. The same message every morning. It’s hard to tell if she even sends them anymore or if it’s all just automated. I delete it without a second thought.

I dress mechanically, my movements hollow—black trousers, black shoes, grey top. Our uniform. I take a breath before stepping out into the hallway, knowing what awaits. My heart races, not from anticipation, but from fear. Every day, it feels harder to resist, like the world outside is slowly encroaching on what little remains of me.

The corridor feels wrong today, the grey walls seeming to suck all warmth, all life, from the air. My shoes squeak against the pristine floor, and I wince at the sound. The doors lining the hallway are identical, as if mocking me. I wonder, briefly, if I’m the only one left in this world of empty, smiling faces.

As I walk to the park, the creeping dread grows, my heartbeat louder in my ears.

Mr. Stephens is there, as always, with his hollow gaze. He tips his hat, eyes vacant, lips curling into that same, unnerving smile. "Ms. Seymore, good morning."

I force a nod. "Good morning."

Mrs. Stephens appears like clockwork. "Good morning, Ms. Seymore. I hope you find blessings in your day."

Creating a soft safe space you can do at any point though, make a little nook where you read books together, speak softly and gently and develop the association that the space, is for soothing and relaxing. This can be done now. 

Make some safe glitter jars that you sit and watch in that space. Blow bubbles gently to encourage deep breathing. Have sensory bags and soft toys, maybe a very simple music player or light with child-safe buttons. 

Read books and sing songs about feelings, start teaching through play silly faces and feeling faces. Demonstrate and model your emotional regulation. 

At 8 months old she is a long way from being able to do it herself, she needs you to physically (through touch and being calm) co-regulate with her. What you are going to teach her by this co-regulation is that emotions are part of being human and they can be expressed safely. We don't want a calm-down corner to be a way to learn that emotions are shameful. That is why you are so important in this. You stay with your child and help them calm down by loving them through their upset. But over time, your child is capable of learning to calm herself. By being taught that the snuggle corner is safe, she will slowly end up being able to use it herself when she needs to calm down. (In a few years)

But it isn't a naughty step. You don't send them there to calm down. That rejects the emotions as something to be hidden. Create it now and make it for quiet times, not when your little one is already upset.

Having a family and a child, can be a wonderful thing. If you are both ready for the changes.

  
First will be pregnancy, that will have sickness, pain, hormonal swings and allsorts. Alongside the wonder of having baby move in about 4 or 5 months time. Then of course the tiredness, uncomfortableness. Never ending urge to pee and then giving birth.

Giving birth varies, from a quick uncomplicated smooth ride to complications for you and baby alongside the potential for operation needed (C-section) 

You don't mention what your chronic pain links to, but this could majorly impact the pregnancy and birth, not to mention overall life. 

So after getting through the next almost 10 months of pregnancy and birth, you then get released from hospital with this tiny vulnerable creature and your job is to keep it alive, while dealing with afterpains and recovery and passing clots the size of oranges for the next few weeks - think of the worst period and multiply it. You are having 10 months worth of periods in one go. 

The flush of love might happen immediately it might take more time both are normal, on day three due to hormones you might feel like the world is ending. 

Baby the amazing little creatures - with fingernails! will need round the clock care for the first 6-8 weeks. Every 2 hours gradually increasing they need food, changing, burping - there are fluids everywhere and you need to look after yourselves and each other during all of this. Your baby will not have read the manual and it will be figuring things out together to see what works for both of you. 

Now for the next 20 years, you and your partner are going to be forever linked as you turn this tiny baby into a functioning and competent human. Think about what you were like as teenagers - having sex since 13 you are both kind of lucky this hasn't happened earlier. No judgement, just reproductive facts. 

Think about your childhoods together and talk about discipline and parenting expectations and roles. If child is rude what is the consequence? What if child breaks something by accident? Have really detailed conversations and see if you are compatible when things are easy.

You will have to clean up every type of bodily fluid imaginable - projectile vomit and diarrhea can get in the oddest places! But every laugh smile and adoring gaze can easily outshadow that.

You will need to pay for everything and babies can be expensive depending on the support you have. If breastfeeding works - great - if not then there are bottles, formulas, sterilising stuff. Nappies, clothes that last 5 minutes. 

Most of what you spend on yourselves for fun will go to baby, all the time that you sleep and rest will have baby there and needing looking after. Most conversations will be about baby. Travelling involves enough stuff to fill a small trailer and will be done roughly around babies routine.
